title: Pilot
note: Episode 1, played as an interactive sitcom (web/src/Pilot.tsx plays `show`, scene by scene): the cast act out the four boxes of a web app, argue each of four decisions on stage, and the player picks a side; a pick that fails Thursday plays a flash-forward and the champion says when it would be right. Hours, prices and counts are illustrative.

beats.say: Welcome to the house. Ten percent of whatever you make under this roof is mine. In return, I make you a founder. There's no paperwork. There's a little paperwork.
That's Aleister Jr. It runs on Aleister, my server in the garage. It writes code all night and it has never once asked a question.
Questions slow me down!
... Two hundred thousand. On Thursday, two hundred of my diners try Forkcast. On whatever they carry.
Some have iPhones, some have Android phones, some will be at their desks on laptops. If they can all use it and it finds them a table, he invests.
Eight hours! I know exactly what to build. I'll start now!
Before it builds anything: the whiteboard. There are decisions here we can't take back on Friday.
Every app you'll ever build is some version of four boxes. I'll draw them.
Boxes are for people who can't visualise. We act it out. I did two weeks of improv. I was asked to leave for being too good.
I'll be the server. Obviously. The brains.
The backend is more of a kitchen. Diners never go in. It holds our rules and our secrets, and only we can change it.
Then I'm the phone. The face of the operation. The pretty one.
The frontend is everything the diner sees and taps. It runs on their phone or laptop, not on ours.
Could I be the database? I already write everything down. People have asked me to stop.
The database is the reservations book. Anything that has to last, like every booking, gets written down there.
I'll be the AI model. Another company. I charge by the question and I don't care about you.
An expert we phone. We pay for every call, and our secret key proves the bill is ours.
Walter types “quiet for six, Friday” and taps Search. The phone packs it into a request.

beats.prompt: Danesh is holding Walter's search. Who does he hand it to?

gilroy.say: You can't phone me without our secret key. You'd have to carry it around. In public. Hold that thought.

gerard.say: Diners don't write in the book themselves. Imagine the handwriting. Imagine the lies.

beats.say: It crosses the internet to forkcast dot app. DNS turns that name into the server's address. HTTPS seals it, so nobody on the café Wi-Fi can read it.
I check it's a real request. Then I phone the expert. With the key, from my pocket.
Five restaurants. That'll be two cents. I'll be keeping the envelope. No, I won't.
Three of those five have a table for six on Friday. And I've written down that Walter asked. Forever.
Nonna's back room. About one second, round trip. The face takes the credit.
Every tap that fetches something is one trip round that loop.
I'd like it noted that the brains did most of the work.
Three apps! iPhone in Swift, Android in Kotlin, and one for laptops. Native, like the real companies!
Three apps is three sets of bugs, and every fix queues for two app stores.
Then one codebase that becomes both phone apps. React Native. Cross-platform. The grown-up answer.
And the forty-four diners on laptops?
Laptops are a niche.
Nobody types a web address any more. If it isn't in the App Store, it isn't a real company.
A web app. One site. Opens from Walter's link on anything with a browser, and a fix reaches everyone on their next tap.
Or the same web app, installable. An icon on the home screen, and reminders before dinner. An hour more.
They're all real choices. The question is which one fits Thursday. Every must on the board needs a yes.

beats.prompt: Everyone turns to you. Where does Forkcast run?

native.say: Forty-four of Walter's diners are on laptops. There's nothing for them to open.
And the iPhone fix is in App Store review! Usually about a day!
Fine. Native is right when the phone itself is the product: the camera, background location, a place in the store. Not for Thursday.
I still think we should tell the press it's an app.

cross.say: The diners had to install a test app before they could install ours. Half gave up. The laptops couldn't open anything.
Also the twelve hours of building ran out at hour eight! Mathematically!
Cross-platform is right when you need both phones and the stores, and you have the time. One codebase is still two store reviews.

web.say: Start on the web unless there's a reason not to. Make it installable when reminders matter; go native when the phone itself is the product.

pwa.say: It passes. But reminders aren't Thursday's problem, so that's an hour we didn't strictly need. Fine.

beats.say: For the record, I'll be telling people at parties that it's an app.
Good news: we don't need a server at all! The app talks straight to the AI model. Fewer boxes. Simplest possible!
So I've been fired from my own metaphor. Wonderful.
Key, please.
Aleister put it in the app. So, I have it. In my... app pocket.
Let me look at the app.

beats.prompt: Every diner's browser downloads this. Tap the line that gives it away.

key.say: That's our key. Every diner downloads it with the app. Anyone can copy it and run their own projects on our bill.
Copied. I'm mining cryptocurrency on your bill now. Kidding. Probably.

beats.say: The brains return.
The phone can't keep a secret. That's what the box in the middle is for.
I've made sticky notes. Five pieces of Forkcast. Tell me where each one lives.

beats.prompt: Gerard holds up: “Search box and buttons.” Where does it live?
“The AI model's secret key.” Where does it live?

beats.say: Screens on the phone, rules and secrets on the server, what must last in the database.

beats.sub: Build the backend, or rent it?

beats.say: We write our own. Node, TypeScript, our own server. Real engineers build.
Then real engineers do logins, backups and updates at three in the morning. Six hours of it before Thursday.
Or we rent the pieces. Supabase: a real Postgres database, logins and storage, ready made. Our rules go in small server functions.
Renting is someone else's server with a nicer website. Sometimes that's exactly what you want.
Or I make the whole thing in an AI app builder in one hour! Live before lunch!
Will it talk to the restaurants' own booking systems? Next month?
It will try very, very hard.
Look at what the platform left us in hours, and the musts. Then pick.

beats.prompt: Everyone turns to you. Build it, rent it, or let the builder make it?

own.sub: Thursday, 3:58pm · if we'd built our own

own.say: Two more hours! Logins are nearly... Walter's diners are here, aren't they.
None of these is wrong forever. Many teams rent first and build their own pieces as they grow.
Our own backend is right when the rules outgrow anything you can rent. Not in four hours.

builder.sub: A month later · if the app builder made it

builder.say: The builder couldn't run our booking-fee rule on a server, so the price gets checked on the diner's phone. Diners have noticed. Most now pay nothing.
And Nonna's booking system wants to connect. The builder doesn't do that, and we can't change how it works underneath.
I could build it again somewhere else! From the beginning! Happily!
Fine. App builders are right for a prototype you'll throw away, or a tool just for us. Not for this.

baas.say: Renting is faster and costs control; lock-in is how hard it is to move out later. Supabase is Postgres underneath, so we could.

beats.say: Here's the plan! Every line is a choice you made. Mostly.
Every line of a plan should belong to one of the boxes. Whoever's playing that box claims it.

beats.prompt: One line on Aleister's plan nobody can claim. Which one would you question?

bad.say: Wait. Nobody claims that one, because it's coming to me.
In Next.js, a setting whose name starts NEXT_PUBLIC goes into what every browser downloads. The key is headed for the phone again.
Tell Aleister: the key stays on the server.
Fixed! I named it public because... I see it now.
Into the brains' pocket. Where it belongs.

beats.say: Merging! Building! See you Thursday!
Did we win? We won. I could feel it.
Here's what we decided, and why. One line per big decision. Future you will thank present you.
Walter's cheque. Two hundred thousand. He wrote one word on the back: “Boring.” From Walter, that's a compliment.
Forkcast is a beautiful idea. Hubbub would like to give it a home. Four million dollars, today.
Why pay four million for something he could build in a month? Unless he wants nobody to build it.
... My two hundred thousand stands. One question. Where do people sign up?
A page for people to sign up on. By Saturday, for Ulrich's party. I'm going to be sick.

platform.label: WHAT TO TELL YOUR AI
platform.plain: One site that opens from a link on any device and lays itself out for phones first. A fix reaches everyone on their next tap.
platform.eg: Real terms: web app; progressive web app (PWA) if it's installable; native or cross-platform apps when the phone is the product.

rule.label: THE RULE
rule.plain: Everything sent to a browser or a phone can be read and changed by whoever holds it. Secrets and rules stay on the server.
rule.eg: Real term: a secret key (or API key). What to tell your AI: “keep keys on the server.”

backend.label: NEW WORDS
backend.plain: Renting a backend (a backend-as-a-service) is faster and costs some control. Lock-in is how hard it is to move out later.
backend.eg: What to tell your AI: “Supabase for the database and logins; our rules in server functions.”

stack.label: NEW WORD
stack.plain: The list of tools a plan uses, layer by layer. Before you merge, put every line on the map. A line you can't place is a question to ask.
stack.eg: Real term: environment variable, a setting kept outside the code. NEXT_PUBLIC_ ones are sent to every browser.
